ION performed parametric 2 testing with ICE-21™ over approximately 350 hours of testing from October 2023 to December 2023, followed by over 800 hours of long-term testing from January 2024 to February 2024. ION captured approximately 580 tCO with ICE-21™, achieving capture efficiencies as high as 99%. Due to a 2 discharge permitting issue (that was resolved at the start of the ICE-31® campaign), ION was unable to operate the direct contact cooler (DCC) blowdown stream during the ICE-21™ campaign, which prevented ION from cooling the flue gas below the dew point. The inability to cool below the dew point of the flue gas prevented ION from achieving optimal performance with ICE-21™. Steady- ION Clean Energy iv DE-FE0031950: FINAL PROJECT REPORT state operations with ICE-21™ were run continuously while parametric testing was performed in 12- hour weekday-only shift work. Emissions during the MEA and ICE-21™ campaigns were measured using a Gasmet FTIR Portable Gas Analyzer. The Gasmet continuously measured CO , water content, ammonia, formaldehyde, 2 amine emissions, and oxygen. MEA emissions showed relatively high ammonia readings (above 20 ppm NH ) while all other emissions were at or below the Gasmet limit of detection (LOD). All ICE- 3 21™ emissions, including ammonia, were at or below the Gasmet LOD. The ICE-31® campaign began in February 2024 and concluded in February 2025 with 24-hour seven- day-a-week operations. ICE-31® had over 2250 hours of parametric testing from February 2024 to July 2024, followed by nearly 4000 hours of long-term steady-state testing concluding in February 2025. ION captured 2500 tCO with ICE-31® over the entire campaign and achieved capture 2 efficiencies as high as 99.4%. At such high capture efficiencies, the flue gas leaving the absorber contains approximately 250 to 300 ppmv CO , which is less than ambient air. ICE-31® exhibited 2 solvent stability in a high-oxygen environment with very little solvent makeup throughout the campaign. ICE-31® emissions were too low for the Gasmet and were measured using a state-of- the-art, research-grade, Proton-Transfer-Reaction Time-of-Flight (PTR-TOF) mass spectrometer. For the last month of testing, ION focused on testing the aged solvent at multiple commercially relevant flue gas inlet temperatures. Emissions of acetaldehyde, the only detected Hazardous Air Pollutant (HAP), were generally below 2 to 3 ppbv with the highest reading around 7 ppbv. Other Volatile Organic Compound (VOC) emissions associated with the solvent were generally below 1 ppbv with the highest reading around 3 ppbv. These results further demonstrate the excellent emissions performance that can be achieved with ICE-31® on NGCC facilities. The results confirm and expand ION’s expectations that ICE-31® is an exceptional solvent for flue gases with high oxidative potential, such as NGCC facilities. The impressive results from the ENTP pilot further demonstrate the readiness of ICE-31® as a viable, commercially deployable carbon capture technology.
